rv.q: The production that opened on Wednesday at the Park Avenue Armory, directed by Icke and starring Juliet Stevenson, is less the exercise in Shavian moral argument that Schnitzler rather airily called a comedy than a tragic thought experiment about the failure of identity politics.
It’s handsome and well-acted, but what’s positioned as a grand thought experiment quickly becomes slick and self-congratulatory.
All of it adds up to a riveting night at the theater.

The quality of Icke’s writing and the stunning performances from the company, particularly Stevenson, keep the play from becoming an episode of Grey’s Anatomy; in less capable hands, it easily could’ve.
Two current Off-Broadway productions offer an unblinkered diagnosis of the current divided state and while it may not provide a pretty picture, these X-rays are illuminating and gripping.

For this galvanizing production imported from London by the Park Avenue Armory, Stevenson, who’s onstage every minute (including a good chunk of the intermission, like Ben Platt in Parade ), delivers a brilliant tour-de-force turn that demands to be seen.
The intense central performance by Stevenson, who throws herself truly, madly, deeply into the demanding role, needs no accompaniment.
Still, watching Stevenson navigate such a difficult role is consistently astonishing.
But around her, the play feels a tired and claustrophobic rhetorical parlor game, echoing the bafflement we see on Stevenson’s face.

It turns complex intellectual debates into a tense and intriguing drama that serves as a vehicle for the nuanced, intense, eminently watchable performance of Juliet Stevenson in the title role, her first on a New York stage in twenty years.
Icke has loaded his new play with tons of ideas, lots of speeches and, possibly, one character.
The cumulative effect of all this strenuous, sub-Shavian oratory and posturing is, first, giggles, and then the realization that Wolff is unhinged and absurdly unprofessional.
It’s unmissable for any theater lover.
But her comeuppance feels out of proportion to her supposed sins.

cn.t: Icke's provocative adaptation tackles timely issues with intelligence, anchored by Juliet Stevenson's powerhouse performance, though critics split on whether its verbose, debate-heavy approach is engrossing or exhausting.
